paragraphs: The most important event that can mark the history of a people is the outbreak of a war. In war a people struggles against foreign nations, with the energy of a single man, to defend its very existence. A skilled government, the good sense of the community, and the natural attachment men feel for their country may be enough to keep the peace within a district and to promote its internal prosperity. But a nation can carry on a great war only by making more numerous and more painful sacrifices, and to suppose that great numbers of men will comply of their own accord with these demands of the state is to show an ignorance of mankind. Every people that has had to sustain a long and serious war has therefore been led to increase the power of its government. Those that failed to do so were conquered. A long war almost always leaves nations the wretched choice of being abandoned to ruin by defeat or to despotism by victory. War therefore exposes the weakness of a government most plainly and most alarmingly; and I have shown that the inherent defect of federal governments is that they are weak.

The Federal system lacks every kind of centralized administration, and the central government itself is also imperfectly organized. This is always a major cause of inferiority when the nation faces other countries that are governed by a single authority. Under the Federal Constitution of the United States, in which the central government has more real strength, this evil is still very much felt. An example will make the matter clear to the reader.

The Constitution gives Congress the right to call out the militia to execute the laws of the Union, suppress insurrections, and repel invasions; and another article declares that the President of the United States is the commander-in-chief of the militia. In the war of 1812 the President ordered the militia of the Northern States to march to the frontiers. But Connecticut and Massachusetts, whose interests were harmed by the war, refused to obey the order. They argued that the Constitution authorizes the Federal Government to call out the militia in case of insurrection or invasion, but that in this instance there was neither invasion nor insurrection. They added that the same Constitution that gave the Union the right to call out the militia reserved to the States the right to name the officers. Consequently (as they understood the clause) no officer of the Union had any right to command the militia, even in wartime, except the President in person; and in this case the militia had been ordered to join an army commanded by someone else. These absurd and harmful doctrines were endorsed not only by the governors and the legislative bodies but also by the courts of justice in both States, and the Federal Government was forced to raise the troops it needed elsewhere. *v

v [ Kent’s “Commentaries,” vol. i. p. 244. I have chosen an example that relates to a time after the adoption of the present Constitution. If I had gone back to the days of the Confederation, I could have given still more striking instances. The whole nation was at that time in a state of enthusiastic excitement; the Revolution was embodied in a man who was the idol of the people; but even then Congress had, to tell the truth, no resources at all at its disposal. Troops and supplies were constantly lacking. The best-designed projects failed in the execution, and the Union, which was always on the verge of destruction, was saved far more by the weakness of its enemies than by its own strength. [All doubt as to the powers of the Federal Executive was, however, removed by its efforts in the Civil War, and those powers were largely extended.]]

With all the relative excellence of its laws, the American Union has only one safeguard against the dissolution that a great war would bring about: it is unlikely to suffer that calamity. The Union lies in the center of an immense continent that offers a boundless field for human industry, and it is almost as cut off from the rest of the world as if its frontiers were surrounded by the ocean. Canada has only a million inhabitants, and its population is divided into two hostile nations. The severity of the climate limits the growth of its territory and closes its ports for the six months of winter. From Canada to the Gulf of Mexico there are only a few savage tribes, which retreat, dying out as they go, before six thousand soldiers. To the south the Union touches the empire of Mexico, and it is from there that serious hostilities may one day be expected. But for a long time to come, the uncivilized state of Mexican society, the corruption of its morals, and its extreme poverty will keep that country from ranking high among nations. *w As for the Powers of Europe, they are too far away to be formidable.
w [ [War broke out between the United States and Mexico in 1846, and ended in the conquest of an immense territory, including California.]]
The great advantage of the United States, then, does not lie in a Federal Constitution that allows them to carry on great wars, but in a geographical position that makes such wars extremely unlikely.

No one is more inclined than I am to appreciate the advantages of the federal system, which I regard as one of the arrangements most favorable to human prosperity and freedom. I envy the lot of the nations that have been able to adopt it. But I cannot believe that any confederate peoples could sustain a long or an equal contest against a nation of similar strength whose government was centralized. A people that divided its sovereignty into fractional powers, in the presence of the great military monarchies of Europe, would in my opinion give up its power by that very act, and perhaps its existence and its name. But the position of the New World is so admirable that man has no enemy but himself. To be happy and free, he need only seek the gifts of prosperity and the knowledge of freedom.
